setup: Lie on your back, legs straight
Hands by your sides or under your hips
Press your lower back into the floor
execution: Lift your legs until they point at the ceiling
Keep your lower back down the whole time
Lower slowly to just above the floor
Breathe out as the legs rise
faults: Don't let your lower back arch up
Don't swing to get them up

notes: If your lower back starts to lift as the legs go down, stop the lowering higher up or bend your knees a little.
On a flat bench, hold the bench behind your head and keep the bench steady before you start.
If pain lingers or comes back, stop this exercise and get it checked by a physio or doctor.
stopIf: Pain that changes how you move

guideBrief.cameraNote: Side view at floor level, figure lying along the frame with the head on the left. A thin mat line under the body.

keyPositions.label: Low
keyPositions.describe: Lying on the back, arms by the sides. Legs straight together, heels hovering just above the mat. Lower back flat on the mat.

keyPositions.label: Up
keyPositions.describe: Straight legs raised until they point at the ceiling. Lower back and hips still on the mat.

ikHints: Shoulders, head and hips stay on the mat in every frame
emphasise: Lower back stays pressed to the mat
Slow lowering to just above the floor
doNotShow: Lower back arching off the mat

uncertain.note: StrengthLog lists the hip flexors as a primary muscle, and they do much of the lifting. The catalogue has no hip_flexors word (expansion research Q1), so they are left out rather than mapped to another muscle.
"Leg raise" alone could mean the hanging version for some people. It is JEFIT's name for this floor exercise; an import may still want Ben to confirm it.
